query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a nominally single‐phase high-entropy alloy, service-like conditions (high temperature, high strain rate, and prolonged dwell times) induce subtle, nanoscale grain-boundary chemical fluctuations (trace element segregation without overt intermetallic precipitation) that act as a local weakening mediator. This in-situ formation of nanosegregation degrades boundary cohesion and triggers a brittle failure mechanism distinct from the conventional gross segregation/precipitation seen in traditional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy (e.g., CrCoNi-type system) with a homogeneous solid solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: Perform in-situ high-temperature, high-strain-rate mechanical testing coupled with atomic-scale characterization (3D-APT and high-resolution STEM/EDS/EELS) while systematically varying temperature, strain rate, and dwell time.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant loading: high temperatures (e.g., near upper service limits), high strain rates, and controllable dwell times to simulate prolonged exposure; comparison performed concurrently on a conventional alloy exhibiting known segregation/precipitation-driven brittleness.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale grain-boundary segregation (incipient trace element clustering) that arises under thermal/mechanical activation.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature, high-strain-rate conditions, atomic mobility is enhanced even in a robust high-entropy alloy. This promotes subtle segregation of certain elements at the grain boundaries, locally reducing cohesive strength and providing preferred sites for crack initiation. Unlike conventional alloys, this transition occurs without the formation of gross brittle intermetallic precipitates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline ductile behavior observed prior to segregation, samples exposed to the defined intervention will show the early onset of localized nanosegregation at grain boundaries accompanied by a transition to brittle behavior (e.g., intergranular cracking) at lower strain to failure.
generation.baseline: The high-entropy alloy exhibits uniformly ductile deformation without significant grain-boundary segregation when tested under milder temperature/strain-rate conditions, and conventional alloys show brittle behavior only after well-developed segregation and precipitate formation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under high-temperature service conditions and high strain rates; outside these regimes (e.g., at low temperatures or very slow loading rates), the alloy is predicted to retain its ductility and homogeneous microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold of temperature, strain rate, and dwell time required to trigger the nanosegregation is not precisely defined, and the relative contribution of different alloying elements to the segregation process remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled in-situ mechanical test on two sets of samples: one set being the single-phase high-entropy alloy and the other a conventional alloy known for grain-boundary segregation-induced brittleness. Under incrementally increasing temperature, strain rate, and dwell time, use real-time atomic-scale characterization (3D-APT, STEM/EDS/EELS) to monitor grain-boundary chemistry and correlate structural changes with mechanical response. Document the onset of any nanoscale segregation and correlate it with transition metrics from ductile to brittle behavior.
measurements: Real-time grain-boundary elemental distribution via 3D-APT or STEM/EDS/EELS
Stress–strain response to capture changes in ductility/brittleness
Fractography to determine intergranular or transgranular crack propagation characteristics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy under high-temperature, high-strain-rate conditions does not show a measurable onset of nanoscale grain-boundary segregation prior to brittle failure, or if brittle fracture occurs without any detectable grain-boundary compositional changes (in contrast to the conventional alloy behavior), then the hypothesis is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) contain multiple principal (or major) elements, commonly five or more, in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios, differently from conventional alloys. While the configurational entropy of an alloy increases with the increasing number of alloying elements, multiple principal elements of an HEA lead to high entropy of mixing that thus suppresses the formation of intermetallic compounds [,,]. Therefore, stable solid solution phases, such as face-centered cubic (FCC) phase, body-centered cubic (BCC) phase, and hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase can be obtained [,]. Meanwhile, HEAs have been shown to exhibit outstanding mechanical and chemical properties, such as high strength and hardness [,], exceptional ductility, as well as excellent oxidation and corrosion resistances [], and thus have become potential candidate materials for many challenging industrial applications. The design and application of HEAs require a comprehensive understanding of their properties and underlying deformation mechanisms. decision.trend: Early work on single-phase, compositionally complex alloys such as CrCoNi (PMC4740901) demonstrated notable strength and damage-tolerance even down to cryogenic temperatures, highlighting the promise of high-entropy and medium-entropy alloys for retaining ductility under extreme conditions. Later studies of refractory high-entropy alloys (PMC8446014) uncovered unexpected dislocation mechanisms that yield exceptional high-temperature strength. More recent investigations (PMC10708198) revealed that trace-element segregation and subtle phase separation during aging can degrade mechanical properties, underscoring that even nominally single-phase high-entropy alloys may suffer from boundary-related instabilities over time. Despite clear evidence of suppressed gross intermetallic formation, the precise mechanisms by which local grain-boundary segregation or nanoscale phases might trigger brittle behavior remain poorly understood.
decision.unsolved: It is not yet determined how localized grain-boundary processes—specifically minor segregation or nanoscale precipitation—might destabilize the intrinsically ductile, single-phase high-entropy alloy matrix and cause brittle failure under demanding engineering conditions. The conditions that tip the balance from ductile to brittle modes, and the underlying atomic-scale origins of that transition, remain unresolved.
decision.lever: Use an in situ high-temperature, high-strain-rate mechanical testing platform combined with correlative atomic-scale microscopy (3D-APT and high-resolution STEM/EDS/EELS) on single-phase high-entropy alloys. The test would systematically vary temperatures, strain rates, and dwell times, all representative of engineering service conditions, while tracking the formation of atomic-scale segregation or incipient precipitates along grain boundaries to pinpoint the onset of intergranular embrittlement.
decision.why: This approach directly addresses the open question of whether grain-boundary segregation or subtle boundary-phase formation triggers brittle transitions. Capturing real-time or near-real-time evolution of boundary chemistry and structure under service-like stresses and temperatures provides the critical mechanistic link between local microstructure changes and the macroscale onset of embrittlement, enabling a direct comparison with known segregation-driven brittleness in conventional alloys.
